title: Fire extinguisher: empty it safely, then take the tank, valve and hose
summary: A spent extinguisher gives you a strong tank, a squeeze valve, a gauge and a short hose: the water type becomes a pressure sprayer and a CO2 cylinder stays a sound bottle. Allow about 40 minutes, most of it for emptying it and proving it is empty. The danger is stored pressure, so never open, cut or drill a cylinder that might still be charged.

steps.text: Decide whether to strip it at all. A charged extinguisher with the needle in the green and the pin and seal in place is worth more kept for fighting fires. Strip only units that are empty, discharged, old or damaged, or when you need the tank.

Read the label to find the type. Water: silver stainless body, usually a bike-type (Schrader) valve and a gauge. CO2: black horn on a hard hose, no gauge, thick-walled cylinder. Dry chemical (ABC or BC): soft hose, gauge, powder inside. Foam, wet chemical, halon and other clean-agent types say so on the label. Leave halon and clean-agent units sealed. If you can't tell what is inside, don't open it.
Look it over. Leave alone any cylinder with a bulge, a deep dent, rust pits, a corroded neck or a damaged valve.
steps.warn: A weakened cylinder can burst when it is knocked or opened. Don't hammer, drop, heat or carry it around: leave it where it is.

steps.text: Take it outdoors onto open ground, away from people, animals, buildings, vehicles and water, with the wind at your back. Put on safety glasses and gloves, and a cloth or dust mask over your nose and mouth for powder types.

Pull the pin (cut the plastic tamper seal first). Aim the nozzle at bare ground, hold the unit firmly upright and squeeze the handle fully. Keep squeezing until the flow stops and the hissing dies away. That takes about 10-30 seconds for powder and CO2 and about a minute for water.
steps.warn: Never aim it at anyone. A CO2 horn gets cold enough to freeze skin: hold the handle only. Never discharge any type indoors, in a vehicle or in a pit: CO2 pushes out the air and powder fills the lungs.

steps.text: Water types with a Schrader valve: when the water stops, press the valve core with a small screwdriver tip to let the last of the air out. Stand to the side while you do it.

Wait 15-30 minutes outside. A CO2 cylinder is freezing after discharge and can hold a little dry ice that builds pressure again as it warms, so wait until the frost has gone and it feels the same as the air. Then squeeze the handle again: you must get no hiss and no puff. Check the gauge reads zero. Weigh CO2 and powder cylinders: the weight should match the empty weight stamped on the collar.
steps.warn: Don't trust the gauge on its own: they stick and clog. A second squeeze with no hiss, plus the right empty weight, is better proof. If it still hisses or weighs too much, discharge again and wait again.

steps.text: Fix the empty cylinder so it can't tip or turn: lash it upright to a post, or grip the body in a bench vice with wood pads. Don't squeeze a thin-walled body hard enough to dent it.

Loosen the valve a quarter turn anticlockwise with a large adjustable wrench on the valve body, not on the handle, gauge or hose. Stop and listen. Silence: carry on a quarter turn at a time. Any hiss: tighten it again at once, step back and let it vent for longer. On a CO2 cylinder you can skip this step and keep the valve fitted.
steps.warn: A hiss, a pop or a stuck valve means there is still pressure. Never free it with heat or a hammer, or lengthen the wrench with a pipe. Tighten it back and leave it alone.

steps.text: Lift out the valve with its siphon tube, keeping the small O-ring on it. Unscrew the hose and the gauge if you want them. Rinse the valve in clean water, work the handle a few times and let it dry.

Tip out what's left in the cylinder onto bare ground, away from wells, streams and crops, with your mask on. Dry powder is a fine irritant dust: bag it or bury it. Rinse the empty tank twice with clean water. Don't drink water that came out of an extinguisher unless the label says plain water.
Mark the tank 'EMPTY, VENTED' so nobody mistakes it for a charged one. Store cylinders upright, out of sun and heat, and keep the valve, hose and O-ring together in one bag.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Water extinguisher tank.** A stainless tank of about 9 litres built to hold air pressure, with a Schrader valve to pump it up. Refill it with clean water, pump it up with a bike pump and stay in the green on the gauge: a pressure sprayer for washing, watering and putting out small fires, or a pressurised camp shower (see build_solar_shower).
- **CO2 cylinder.** A thick-walled bottle made for very high pressure. Kept whole, with its valve, it is a strong bottle. Treat any refill as a job for someone with proper equipment, and don't fill it with air yourself.
- **Squeeze valve.** A quick on/off valve with its own handle that holds pressure: handy on any home-made sprayer or air-over-water tank.
- **Hose and gauge.** A short hose, and a pressure gauge that works on any small pressure tank (check its range before you rely on it).

## Dry powder, foam and other types

- The body of a dry-powder or foam unit is a low-pressure steel tank. Once vented, opened and rinsed, the tank, valve and gauge are used the same way as the water type, except the tank often has no Schrader valve.
- Foam and wet chemical agents are soaps and chemicals. Empty them on bare ground downhill of any water you might drink, and rinse the tank well before storing anything in it.

## Cartridge-operated types

Some units have a separate small gas cartridge in the head or beside it, and the main body is not under pressure until the cartridge is punctured. Don't press the puncture lever. Unscrew the cartridge first, keep it sealed and treat it like a small CO2 cylinder.

## What to leave

- Halon and other clean-agent units: leave them sealed and use them as extinguishers.
- Any cylinder that is damaged, rusted through or has a bad valve.
- Never cut, drill or weld any extinguisher body, vented or not.
